Stop and surface blockers rather\n> than guessing. Do not claim success without command evidence from the current repo.\n> Machine-readable install spec: [`agent-install.json`](./agent-install.json)\n\n## Table of Contents\n\n- [Prerequisites: what must exist before you start](#prerequisites)\n- [Phase 1: Auth and private registry](#phase-1-auth-and-private-registry)\n- [Phase 2: Install harness globally](#phase-2-install-harness-globally)\n- [Phase 3: Init scaffold](#phase-3-init-scaffold)\n- [Phase 3b: Migrate away from GitHub Actions (if applicable)](#phase-3b-migrate-away-from-github-actions)\n- [Phase 4: mise tool baseline](#phase-4-mise-tool-baseline)\n- [Phase 5: CircleCI environment variables](#phase-5-circleci-environment-variables-and-github-secrets)\n- [Phase 6: Branch protection](#phase-6-branch-protection)\n- [Phase 7: Greptile setup](#phase-7-greptile-setup)\n- [Phase 8: Memory layer bootstrap](#phase-8-memory-layer-bootstrap)\n- [Phase 9: Validate end-to-end](#phase-9-validate-end-to-end)\n- [What harness init scaffolds (file inventory)](#what-harness-init-scaffolds)\n- [What is enforced, adaptable, and optional](#what-is-enforced-adaptable-and-optional)\n- [Capability boundaries](#capability-boundaries)\n- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)\n\n---\n\n## Prerequisites\n\nConfirm these exist before starting. If any are missing, surface the gap and stop.\n\n| Requirement | Check command | Required |\n|---|---|---|\n| `node` ≥ 24 | `node --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `pnpm` ≥ 10 | `pnpm --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `git` | `git --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `jq` | `jq --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `rg` (ripgrep) | `rg --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `fd` | `fd --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `mise` | `mise --version` | ✅ mandatory |\n| `gh` CLI | `gh --version` | Required for branch-protect + GitHub steps |\n| `NPM_TOKEN` env var | `printenv NPM_TOKEN \\| wc -c` (must be > 1) | Required for private pkg auth |\n| 1Password session | `op account list` | Required if secrets come from 1Password |\n\n```bash\n# Quick preflight — run this first\nnode --version && pnpm --version && git --version && jq --version && rg --version && fd --version && mise --version\nprintenv NPM_TOKEN | wc -c   # must print a number > 1\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 1: Auth and private registry\n\nharness is a **private** npm package. Auth must be wired before install.\n\n```bash\n# 1. Confirm token is present (do NOT print the value)\nprintenv NPM_TOKEN | wc -c\n\n# 2. Wire token into ~/.npmrc\necho \"//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}\" >> ~/.npmrc\n\n# 3. Verify npm can authenticate\nnpm whoami\n\n# 4. Confirm the package is reachable\nnpm view @brainwav/coding-harness dist-tags --json\n```\n\nIf `npm whoami` fails, the session NPM_TOKEN is stale or invalid. Stop and instruct the\nuser to refresh their 1Password session or re-export the token.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 2: Install harness globally\n\n```bash\n# Preferred: managed via mise (pinned version, login-shell accessible)\nmise install -g npm:@brainwav/coding-harness\n\n# Fallback: direct npm global (same effect)\nnpm install -g @brainwav/coding-harness\n\n# Verify\nharness --version\nharness --help\n```\n\n> **Do not** use `pnpm exec tsx src/cli.ts` in a consumer repo. That path is\n> coding-harness development only. Generated `scripts/check-environment.sh` always\n> expects the global `harness` binary.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 3: Init scaffold\n\nThe `harness init` command scaffolds all governance files. Follow this sequence:\n\n```bash\n# 3.1 — Dry run first (no writes — safe to always run)\nharness init --dry-run\n\n# Review the planned files. If anything looks wrong, STOP.\n\n# 3.2 — Apply (CircleCI is the standard CI provider for this project)\nharness init\n\n# 3.3 — Verify scaffold applied\nharness init --check-updates\n```\n\n> **CI provider:** `circleci` is the default. Do **not** pass `--ci circleci` here:\n> the current CLI treats that extra positional argument as a target directory.\n> Greptile review runs as a **CircleCI job**\n> (`greptile-review`) — no GitHub Actions workflow file is written or required.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 3b: Migrate away from GitHub Actions\n\n**Skip this phase if the project has no `.github/workflows/` directory.**\n\nIf the target repo already has GitHub Actions workflows, use the dedicated migration\ncommand to remove them safely and cut over to CircleCI. This is a staged, reversible\nprocess — do not manually delete workflow files.\n\n```bash\n# 3b.1 — Preview what will change (safe, no writes)\nharness ci-migrate prepare --provider circleci --dry-run\n```\n\nReview the output. Confirm the listed `.github/workflows/` files will be removed and\nthat the CircleCI config is already present (from Phase 3). If anything looks wrong, STOP.\n\n```bash\n# 3b.2 — Apply the migration and create the recovery snapshot\nharness ci-migrate prepare --provider circleci --apply\n\n# 3b.3 — Verify migration is complete (uses the snapshot id from prepare output)\nharness ci-migrate verify --snapshot <snapshot-id>\n\n# 3b.4 — Commit the cutover once verification passes\nharness ci-migrate commit --snapshot <snapshot-id>\n```\n\n**If something goes wrong:**\n\n```bash\n# Roll back to the pre-migration state\nharness ci-migrate abort --snapshot <snapshot-id>\n```\n\n**What `ci-migrate` does:**\n- Removes `.github/workflows/` CI job files that conflict with CircleCI\n- Updates `harness.contract.json` `activeProvider` to `circleci`\n- Updates `.harness/ci-required-checks.json` to CircleCI check names\n- Creates a snapshot so rollback is always available\n- Does **not** touch `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, `CODEOWNERS`, or `ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` — those are PR hygiene, not CI\n\n> **Agent rule:** Never manually delete `.github/workflows/` files. Always use\n> `harness ci-migrate` so the snapshot + rollback path is available.\n\n**Key files every project MUST have after init:**\n\n```\nharness.contract.json               — governance contract (source of truth)\n.harness/ci-required-checks.json    — required CI check list\n.greptile/config.json               — Greptile AI review config (repo-scoped)\n.greptile/rules.md                  — Greptile custom rules\n.greptile/files.json                — Greptile context files\n.circleci/config.yml                — All CI jobs (lint, test, security, greptile-review, release)\n.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md    — PR checklist\nscripts/codex-preflight.sh          — agent preflight script (source at session start)\nscripts/check-environment.sh        — harness env readiness script\n.codex/environments/environment.toml — Codex action blocks\n.mise.toml                          — pinned tool versions\nMakefile                            — canonical task runner\nprek.toml                           — pre-commit/pre-push hook config\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 4: mise tool baseline\n\nAfter init, harness scaffolds `.mise.toml` with required tool versions.\nInstall everything it pins:\n\n```bash\n# 4.1 — Trust the mise config (required first time)\nmise trust .mise.toml\n\n# 4.2 — Install all tools\nmise install\n\n# 4.3 — Verify key binaries are present\nmise list\nharness check-environment --json\n```\n\n**If `harness check-environment` reports missing binaries**, install them:\n\n```bash\nmise install -g cargo:prek\nmise install -g npm:@brainwav/diagram\nmise install -g npm:@argos-ci/cli\nmise install -g npm:@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli\nmise install -g npm:agentation\nmise install -g npm:agentation-mcp\nmise install -g npm:agent-browser\nmise install -g npm:beautiful-mermaid\nmise install -g npm:markdownlint-cli2\nmise install -g npm:wrangler\n```\n\nVerify binaries are reachable in login shells (non-interactive PATH must be correct):\n\n```bash\nzsh -lc 'prek --version && diagram --version && mmdc --version'\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 5: CircleCI environment variables and GitHub secrets\n\n### CircleCI project environment variables\n\nThese are set in **CircleCI project settings → Environment Variables**.\nHarness cannot create them — surface this to the user if any are missing.\n\n| Variable | Purpose | Source |\n|---|---|---|\n| `NPM_TOKEN` | Install `@brainwav/coding-harness` in CI jobs | npm / 1Password |\n| `GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` | `gh` CLI auth for review-gate, PR creation, branch ops | GitHub PAT |\n| `GREPTILE_API_KEY` | Greptile API call in the `greptile-review` CircleCI job | Greptile dashboard |\n| `LINEAR_API_KEY` | Linear issue sync job | Linear settings |\n\nCheck via CircleCI API:\n\n```bash\n# Replace <owner> and <repo>; requires CIRCLE_TOKEN env var\ncurl -s --request GET \\\n  --url \"https://circleci.com/api/v2/project/github/<owner>/<repo>/envvar\" \\\n  --header \"Circle-Token: $CIRCLE_TOKEN\" | jq '[.items[].name]'\n```\n\n> **No GitHub Actions secrets are required.** All CI including Greptile runs through\n> CircleCI. The only GitHub-side configuration is the Greptile GitHub App installation.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 6: Branch protection\n\n```bash\n# Apply branch protection using the harness ecosystem profile\nharness branch-protect \\\n  --token \"$GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN\" \\\n  --owner <owner> \\\n  --repo <repo> \\\n  --ecosystem harness \\\n  --branch main\n```\n\nRequired checks applied by `--ecosystem harness`:\n\n```\npr-template, linear-gate, risk-policy-gate, dependency-scan,\norb-pinning, consistency-drift-health, docs-gate,\nlint, typecheck, test, audit, check, memory, security-scan, Greptile Review\n```\n\n> `dependency-scan` = Trivy SCA (replaces GitHub Actions `dependency-review`)\n> `orb-pinning` = CircleCI orb version enforcement (replaces GitHub Actions `actions-pinning`)\n\nVerify after applying:\n\n```bash\nharness check-authz \\\n  --contract harness.contract.json \\\n  --repo <owner>/<repo> \\\n  --branch main\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 7: Greptile setup\n\nGreptile provides AI code review on every PR. The scaffolded `.greptile/config.json`\nscopes it to this repository only (prevents cross-repo context contamination).\n\n### 7.1 Verify config files exist\n\n```bash\ntest -f .greptile/config.json && echo \"✅ config\" || echo \"❌ missing\"\ntest -f .greptile/rules.md    && echo \"✅ rules\"  || echo \"❌ missing\"\ntest -f .greptile/files.json  && echo \"✅ files\"  || echo \"❌ missing\"\n```\n\n### 7.2 Verify Greptile GitHub App installation\n\n```bash\nharness verify-greptile \\\n  --token \"$GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN\" \\\n  --owner <owner> \\\n  --repo <repo>\n```\n\nIf this fails: instruct the user to install the Greptile GitHub App from\nhttps://app.greptile.com and grant it access to this repository.\n\n### 7.3 Confirm GREPTILE_API_KEY is set in CircleCI\n\nThe `greptile-review` CircleCI job calls the Greptile API directly using\n`GREPTILE_API_KEY`. Verify it is set as a CircleCI project environment variable:\n\n```bash\ncurl -s --request GET \\\n  --url \"https://circleci.com/api/v2/project/github/<owner>/<repo>/envvar\" \\\n  --header \"Circle-Token: $CIRCLE_TOKEN\" | jq '[.items[].name]' | grep GREPTILE\n```\n\nIf missing: ask the user to add `GREPTILE_API_KEY` in CircleCI project settings → Environment Variables.\n\n---\n\n## Phase 8: Memory layer bootstrap\n\nEvery harness-enabled repo uses a per-project memory file for agent learnings.\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p .harness/memory\ntest -f .harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md || cat > .harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md << 'EOF'\n---\nschema_version: 1\npurpose: Per-project agent knowledge base — repo-specific gotchas and hard-won fixes.\nscope: This repo only.\nupdate_policy: |\n  Append after any bug, tool failure, or extra-effort fix specific to this repo.\n  Universal gotchas go in ~/.codex/instructions/Learnings.md instead.\n  Do NOT delete entries. Append only.\n  Format: **YYYY-MM-DD [Agent]:** <problem> → <fix>\n---\n\n# Learnings\n\nRepo-specific agent knowledge base. Append-only.\nEOF\n```\n\nConfirm `.harness/memory/LEARNINGS.md` is gitignored:\n\n```bash\ngrep -q \"\\.harness/memory\" .gitignore && echo \"✅ gitignored\" || echo \"⚠️  add .harness/memory/ to .gitignore\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## Phase 9: Validate end-to-end\n\nRun this validation ladder in order. Stop on first failure and report.\n\n```bash\n# 9.1 — Preflight (repo context, required binaries)\nsource scripts/codex-preflight.sh && preflight_repo\n\n# 9.2 — Environment check (mise tools, harness readiness)\nharness check-environment --json\n\n# 9.3 — Init idempotency (no pending updates)\nharness init --check-updates\n\n# 9.4 — Policy baseline\npnpm check   # or: npm run check\n\n# 9.5 — Greptile (if token available)\nharness verify-greptile --token \"$GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN\" --owner <owner> --repo <repo>\n\n# 9.6 — Authorization (branch protection matches contract)\nharness check-authz --contract harness.contract.json --repo <owner>/<repo> --branch main\n```\n\nAll six steps must pass before the setup is complete.\n\n---\n\n## What harness init scaffolds\n\nFull file inventory — all paths relative to repo root.\n\n### Core governance\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `harness.contract.json` | Governance contract — source of truth for all policy |\n| `.harness/ci-required-checks.json` | Required CI check names |\n| `memory.json` | Harness memory/state file |\n\n### Greptile AI review\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `.greptile/config.json` | AI review config (strictness, rules, repo scope) |\n| `.greptile/rules.md` | Custom review rules |\n| `.greptile/files.json` | Priority context files for review |\n\nGreptile review is triggered via the `greptile-review` job in `.circleci/config.yml`.\nNo GitHub Actions workflow file is needed — the Greptile GitHub App is installed\non the repository and the CircleCI job calls its API.\n\n### CI pipeline (CircleCI)\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `.circleci/config.yml` | All CI: lint, typecheck, test, audit, security-scan, post-merge, auto-release, publish-npm |\n\n### PR and contribution hygiene\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | PR checklist |\n| `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml` | Issue template routing |\n| `.github/CODEOWNERS` | Code ownership |\n| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | Contribution guide |\n\n### Scripts\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `scripts/codex-preflight.sh` | Agent preflight — source at every session start |\n| `scripts/check-environment.sh` | Harness env readiness check |\n| `scripts/setup-git-hooks.js` | Git hook installer |\n| `scripts/validate-commit-msg.js` | Commit message linter |\n| `scripts/check-staged-secrets.sh` | Pre-commit secret scan |\n| `scripts/check-doc-style.sh` | Doc style enforcer |\n| `scripts/check-related-tests.sh` | Test coverage reminder |\n| `scripts/check-semgrep-changed.sh` | Security scan on changed files |\n| `scripts/refresh-diagram-context.sh` | Architecture diagram refresh |\n| `scripts/check-diagram-freshness.sh` | Diagram staleness gate |\n| `scripts/semgrep-pre-push.yml` | Semgrep config for pre-push |\n\n### Tooling config\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `.mise.toml` | Pinned tool versions (node, pnpm, python, uv, prek, diagram, etc.) |\n| `biome.json` | Formatter/linter config (TypeScript projects) |\n| `.gitleaks.toml` | Secret scanning config |\n| `prek.toml` | Pre-commit/pre-push hook config |\n| `Makefile` | Canonical task runner |\n| `.diagramrc` | Diagram generation config |\n\n### Codex agent environment\n\n| File | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| `.codex/environments/environment.toml` | Codex action blocks (auto-generated from package.json scripts) |\n\n---\n\n## What is enforced, adaptable, and optional\n\nUse this table to decide whether to touch a file. When in doubt, check the column.\n\n### Enforced — harness owns these files\n\n`harness init --update` will overwrite these with the latest template. Do not\nhand-edit them — changes will be lost on the next update. Use harness commands to\nchange the values they encode (for example `harness branch-protect` for required checks).\n\n| File | Owned by |\n|---|---|\n| `harness.contract.json` | `harness init` \\u2014 source of truth for all policy |\n| `.harness/ci-required-checks.json` | `harness init` \\u2014 required check list |\n| `memory.json` | `harness init` \\u2014 harness state file |\n| `.circleci/config.yml` | `harness init` \\u2014 full CI pipeline |\n| `scripts/check-environment.sh` | `harness init` \\u2014 generated from tooling baseline |\n| `.codex/environments/environment.toml` | `harness init` \\u2014 **only safe to edit if not harness-autogenerated** |\n\n### Adaptable — harness writes a starter, you own it after\n\nThese are written once by `harness init` but treated as project-owned after that.\n`harness init --update` will **not** overwrite them unless you pass `--force`.\n\n| File | What to customise |\n|---|---|\n| `.greptile/rules.md` | Add project-specific review rules |\n| `.greptile/files.json` | Add priority context files for review |\n| `.greptile/config.json` | Adjust strictness or scope |\n| `.github/CODEOWNERS` | Set actual owners for this repo |\n| `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` | Add project-specific checklist items |\n| `CONTRIBUTING.md` | Add project-specific contribution guidance |\n| `Makefile` | Add project-specific tasks |\n| `biome.json` | Tune lint/format rules for this project |\n| `prek.toml` | Add/remove hooks for this project |\n| `.mise.toml` | Pin additional tools needed by this project |\n| `.gitleaks.toml` | Add project-specific secret scan exclusions |\n| `scripts/codex-preflight.sh` | Add project-specific preflight checks |\n\n### Optional tooling — install only if the project needs it\n\nThese are **not** scaffolded by `harness init`. Install with `mise install -g` if the\nproject uses them. `harness check-environment` will surface which are missing.\n\n| Tool | Install command | When needed |\n|---|---|---|\n| `@brainwav/diagram` | `mise install -g npm:@brainwav/diagram` | Architecture diagram generation |\n| `@argos-ci/cli` | `mise install -g npm:@argos-ci/cli` | Visual regression CI |\n| `@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli` (`mmdc`) | `mise install -g npm:@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli` | Mermaid diagram rendering |\n| `agentation` | `mise install -g npm:agentation` | Agentation annotation CLI |\n| `agentation-mcp` | `mise install -g npm:agentation-mcp` | Agentation MCP server |\n| `agent-browser` | `mise install -g npm:agent-browser` | Deterministic browser automation |\n| `beautiful-mermaid` | `mise install -g npm:beautiful-mermaid` | Styled diagram output |\n| `markdownlint-cli2` | `mise install -g npm:markdownlint-cli2` | Docs linting |\n| `wrangler` | `mise install -g npm:wrangler` | Cloudflare Workers deploy |\n| `prek` | `mise install -g cargo:prek` | Pre-commit/pre-push hooks (required for hooks to run) |\n\n---\n\n## Capability boundaries\n\nHarness **can** do automatically:\n- Scaffold all governance files (`harness init`)\n- Verify repository state (`check-environment`, `check-authz`, `verify-greptile`)\n- Apply branch protection via GitHub API (`harness branch-protect`)\n- Generate Codex environment action blocks from package.json scripts\n- Run policy gates (lint, typecheck, test, audit, docs-gate, risk-policy-gate)\n\nHarness **cannot** do — requires user action:\n- Create or rotate GitHub tokens/PATs or CircleCI environment variables\n- Install the Greptile GitHub App on a repository\n- Create GitHub repository secrets or CircleCI project vars (agent can check; user must set)\n- Bypass branch protection or required review checks\n- Safely overwrite user-customized `.codex/environments/environment.toml` without explicit approval\n\n---\n\n## Troubleshooting\n\n| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |\n|---|---|---|\n| `npm install -g` fails with 403 | `NPM_TOKEN` expired or missing | Re-export from 1Password; verify `npm whoami` |\n| `harness` not found after install | PATH missing `~/.local/bin` or mise shims | Add to `~/.zprofile`: `export PATH=\"$HOME/.local/bin:$(mise shims path):$PATH\"` |\n| `mise install` hangs | FIFO env file issue | Use `op run -- mise install` or source env file directly |\n| `harness check-environment` reports missing binaries | Tool not installed | Run `mise install -g <tool>` for each missing binary |\n| `harness verify-greptile` fails | Greptile App not installed on repo | User must install from app.greptile.com |\n| Branch protection not applying | PAT missing `repo` + `admin:repo_hook` scopes | Re-generate PAT with required scopes |\n| `preflight_repo` fails in zsh | Old `codex-preflight.sh` without zsh guard | Run `harness init --update` to get the fixed version |\n| CircleCI can't authenticate to npm | `NPM_TOKEN` missing from CircleCI project env vars | Set in CircleCI project settings → Environment Variables |\n| CI fails on `npm pack` / missing `dist/` | Build not run before pack | Verify `.circleci/config.yml` has build step before pack |\n\n\n---\n/Users/jamiecraik/dev/Agent-Skills/utilities/coding-harness/references/setup-and-commands.md:\n# Coding Harness setup and command reference\n\n## Table of Contents\n- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)\n- [Command truth source](#command-truth-source)\n- [Install modes](#install-modes)\n- [Bootstrap workflow](#bootstrap-workflow)\n- [Abbreviations](#abbreviations)\n- [Metadata](#metadata)\n- [Invariants](#invariants)\n- [States](#states)\n- [Transition Table (Canonical)](#transition-table-canonical)\n- [Update workflow for existing repos](#update-workflow-for-existing-repos)\n- [Error Handling](#error-handling)\n- [Idempotency](#idempotency)\n- [Execution Modes](#execution-modes)\n- [Dry-Run Simulation](#dry-run-simulation)\n- [Observability Logs](#observability-logs)\n- [Validation Checklist](#validation-checklist)\n- [Executor pseudocode](#executor-pseudocode)\n- [Validation ladder](#validation-ladder)\n- [environment.toml action sync behavior](#environmenttoml-action-sync-behavior)\n- [Command map](#command-map)\n- [Capability boundaries](#capability-boundaries)\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- Node.js `>=24.0.0`\n- `pnpm` (repo package manager)\n- Repository write access for `harness init` template changes\n- For remote GitHub checks, a valid token (GitHub App JWT is preferred when verifying App installation state)\n\n## Command truth source\n\nPrefer runtime command help over stale prose snapshots:\n\n```bash\nharness --help\n```\n\nIf harness is not installed globally in the current shell, use:\n\n```bash\npnpm exec tsx src/cli.ts --help\n```\n\n## Install modes\n\n### Global npm install (required for generated preflight)\n\n```bash\nnpm install -g @brainwav/coding-harness\nharness --help\n```\n\nRecommended managed install:\n\n```bash\nmise install -g npm:@brainwav/coding-harness\n```\n\nRequired private package auth wiring:\n\n```bash\nexport NPM_TOKEN=<token>\n# CircleCI project settings -> Environment Variables:\n#   NPM_TOKEN\n```\n\n### Project-local source CLI (only for coding-harness development)\n\nUse this only when developing inside the `coding-harness` source repository itself.\nGenerated `scripts/check-environment.sh` in consumer repositories does not fall back\nto `pnpm exec tsx src/cli.ts ...`; it requires the global `harness` binary from npm.\n\n## Bootstrap workflow\n\n1. Install dependencies:\n\n## Abbreviations\n| Abbr | Meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| `S` | state |\n| `E` | event |\n| `G` | guard |\n| `A` | action |\n| `N` | next state |\n\n## Metadata\n| Field | Value |\n| --- | --- |\n| `owner` | `TODO` |\n| `max_duration` | `TODO` |\n| `escalation` | `TODO` |\n\n## Invariants\n- TODO invariant 1\n- TODO invariant 2\n\n## States\n```txt\nS0 (non-terminal)\nDONE (terminal)\nFAIL (terminal)\nBLOCKED (terminal)\n```\n\n## Transition Table (Canonical)\n`S | E | G | A | N`\n\n### State machine\n\n```txt\nB0 PREFLIGHT -> B1 DEPS -> B2 INIT_PREVIEW -> B3 INIT_APPLY -> B4 VALIDATE -> B5 READY\n     |             |            |              |\n     +-----------> BX FAIL <----+--------------+\n```\n\n### Transition table (`S | E | G | A | N`)\n\n| S | E | G | A | N |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `B0 PREFLIGHT` | `preflight_ok` | preflight script passes | `source scripts/codex-preflight.sh && preflight_repo` | `B1 DEPS` |\n| `B1 DEPS` | `deps_installed` | `pnpm` available | `pnpm install` | `B2 INIT_PREVIEW` |\n| `B2 INIT_PREVIEW` | `preview_ok` | dry-run exits clean | `harness init --dry-run` | `B3 INIT_APPLY` |\n| `B3 INIT_APPLY` | `init_applied` | templates generated | `harness init` | `B4 VALIDATE` |\n| `B4 VALIDATE` | `checks_pass` | baseline gate passes | `pnpm check` and optional `harness verify-greptile` | `B5 READY` |\n| `B*` | `error` | any guard fails | capture blocker + stop | `BX FAIL` |\n\nExpected scaffold lane in `B3`:\n- `.greptile/config.json`\n- `.greptile/rules.md`\n- `.greptile/files.json`\n- `.github/workflows/greptile-review.yml`\n\n## Update workflow for existing repos\n\n### State machine\n\n```txt\nU0 CHECK -> U1 PREVIEW -> U2 APPLY -> U3 VALIDATE -> U4 DONE\n   |          |           |             |\n   +--------> UX FAIL <---+-------------+\n```\n\n### Transition table (`S | E | G | A | N`)\n\n| S | E | G | A | N |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| `U0 CHECK` | `updates_found` | update check runs | `harness init --check-updates` | `U1 PREVIEW` |\n| `U1 PREVIEW` | `preview_ok` | dry-run output reviewed | `harness init --dry-run --update` | `U2 APPLY` |\n| `U2 APPLY` | `apply_ok` | selected update strategy confirmed | `harness init --update` (or `--interactive`) | `U3 VALIDATE` |\n| `U2 APPLY` | `tracked_apply` | rollback tracking requested | `harness init --track` before apply | `U3 VALIDATE` |\n| `U3 VALIDATE` | `checks_pass` | validation ladder passes | run `pnpm check` (+ deep gate if needed) | `U4 DONE` |\n| `U*` | `migration_or_rollback` | contract transition needed | `harness init --migrate` or `harness init --rollback` | `U0 CHECK` |\n| `U*` | `error` | any guard fails | capture blocker + stop | `UX FAIL` |\n\n## Error Handling\n- `VALIDATION_ERROR`: invalid command invocation or malformed workflow input.\n- `BLOCKED_DEPENDENCY`: missing binaries/auth/dependencies required by guards.\n- `POLICY_FAIL`: required validation/policy gates fail.\n- `SYSTEM_ERROR`: runtime/process failures.\n\n## Idempotency\n- Key: `<lane>|<repo>|<event>|<target_state>`.\n- Re-running preview and validate steps must be side-effect free.\n- Apply steps should be replay-safe with guard checks.\n\n## Execution Modes\n- `STRICT`: stop on first violation/failure.\n- `ADVISORY`: collect warnings and continue where safe.\n\n## Dry-Run Simulation\n- No file mutations or external writes; no side effects.\n- Deterministic transition trace output based on guard evaluation.\n\n## Observability Logs\n`workflow_id, transition_code, from_state, to_state, correlation_id, result`\n\n## Validation Checklist\n- every non-terminal state has >=1 outbound transition\n- deterministic `(S,E)` handling\n- failure paths route to `FAIL`/`BLOCKED`\n- terminal states (`B5 READY`, `U4 DONE`) have no outbound transitions\n\n## Executor pseudocode\n\n```txt\nrun bootstrap or update lane\nfor each transition row, execute action when guard is true\nstop on first error transition and emit unblock guidance\n```\n\n## Validation ladder\n\nBaseline gate:\n\n```bash\npnpm check\n```\n\nDeep gate (when runtime behavior, contract behavior, or artifact handling changed):\n\n```bash\npnpm test:deep\n```\n\nSituational governance checks:\n\n```bash\nharness check-authz --contract harness.contract.json --repo <owner/repo> --branch <branch>\nharness check-environment --contract harness.contract.json --attestation artifacts/check-environment-attestation.json\nharness docs-gate --mode advisory --json\nharness tooling-audit --path <directory> --format table\n```\n\n## environment.toml action sync behavior\n\n`harness init` generates `.codex/environments/environment.toml` with:\n\n- Setup script block using the detected package manager.\n- Four canonical actions: `Tools`, `Run`, `Debug`, `Test`.\n- Dynamic per-script action blocks (for each `package.json` script), with icon inference:\n  - `tool`\n  - `run`\n  - `debug`\n  - `test`\n\nImportant constraints:\n\n- Auto-update is safe by default only for harness-autogenerated files.\n- Existing custom/non-autogenerated environment files should be treated as user-owned and not silently overwritten.\n- Missing `run` / `debug` / `test` scripts get explicit failing placeholder commands to prevent false success.\n\n## Command map\n\n### Setup and governance\n\n- `harness init`\n- `harness init --check-updates`\n- `harness init --update`\n- `harness init --migrate`\n- `harness init --rollback`\n- `harness branch-protect`\n- `harness verify-greptile`\n- `harness request-greptile-review`\n- `harness check-authz`\n- `harness check-environment`\n- `harness docs-gate`\n- `harness org-audit`\n- `harness tooling-audit`\n- `harness preset`\n- `harness ci-migrate`\n\n### Risk and policy gates\n\n- `harness risk-tier`\n- `harness policy-gate` (alias: `harness risk-policy-gate`)\n- `harness preflight-gate`\n- `harness diff-budget`\n- `harness review-gate`\n- `harness evidence-verify`\n- `harness silent-error`\n- `harness observability-gate`\n- `harness drift-gate`\n- `harness pr-template-gate`\n- `harness license-gate`\n\n### Documentation and planning hygiene\n\n- `harness gardener`\n- `harness brainstorm-gate`\n- `harness plan-gate`\n- `harness prompt-gate`\n- `harness blast-radius`\n- `harness memory-gate`\n\n### Context and remediation loops\n\n- `harness context`\n- `harness search`\n- `harness index-context`\n- `harness context-health`\n- `harness remediate`\n- `harness replay`\n\n### Pilot and operations\n\n- `harness gap-case`\n- `harness pilot-evaluate`\n- `harness pilot-rollback`\n- `harness automation-run`\n- `harness simulate`\n- `harness ui:fast`\n- `harness ui:verify`\n- `harness ui:explore`\n\n### Intake and workflow governance\n\n- `harness linear`\n- `harness linear-gate`\n- `harness workflow-generate`\n\n## Capability boundaries\n\nHarness can:\n\n- Scaffold governance templates and maintain them over time.\n- Enforce policy checks and report structured pass/fail outcomes.\n- Verify expected repository setup (including Greptile config, workflow checks, and npmrc guidance).\n- Generate Codex environment action blocks from live project scripts.\n\nHarness cannot:\n\n- Create or rotate GitHub credentials/tokens for you.\n- Replace repository-specific engineering judgment or business logic testing.\n- Bypass required checks, rulesets, or review independence policies.\n- Safely overwrite user-customized non-autogenerated environment templates without explicit direction.\n\n\n---\n/Users/jamiecraik/dev/Agent-Skills/utilities/circleci/references/raw-docs-md/docs-guides-migrate-migrating-from-github.md:\nTitle: Migrate from GitHub Actions - CircleCI to CircleCI\n\nMigrate from GitHub Actions\n===========================\n\n[4 months ago](https://github.com/circleci/circleci-docs/commit/3801be10273452515d580f25490470822e49a48f)\n\nCloud Server v4+\n\nMarkdown\n*   [View markdown](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/index.md)\n*    Copy markdown \n\n### On This Page\n\n*   [Concepts](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#concepts)\n*   [Jobs and workflows](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#jobs-and-workflows)\n*   [Actions vs. orbs](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#actions-vs-orbs)\n*   [Runners vs. executors](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#runners-vs-executors)\n*   [Configuration comparison](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#configuration-comparison)\n\nThis document provides an overview of how to migrate from GitHub Actions to CircleCI.\n\nThe [CircleCI configuration translator](https://circleci.com/developer/tools/configTranslator) provides a way to convert your GitHub Actions or GitLab config into a CircleCI `config.yml` file. The configuration translator is currently in open preview.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#concepts)Concepts\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#jobs-and-workflows)Jobs and workflows\n\nBoth GitHub Actions and CircleCI share similar concepts around \"jobs\" and \"workflows\". A workflow is an end-to-end flow of connected jobs, which in turn consist of commands to achieve an atomic task (for example, \"run unit tests\" or \"build a Docker image\").\n\nCircleCI differs primarily in configuration syntax, setting up workflow and job dependencies in a separate section as opposed to inline in the job.\n\n| GitHub | CircleCI |\n| --- | --- |\n| ``` name: My GitHub Actions Workflow on: [push] jobs: job_1: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # job steps job_2: needs: job_1 runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: # job steps ``` yaml | ``` jobs: job_1: executor: my-ubuntu-exec steps: # job steps job_2: executor: my-ubuntu-exec steps: # job steps workflows: my_workflow: jobs: - job_1 - job_2: requires: - job_1 ``` yaml |\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#actions-vs-orbs)Actions vs. orbs\n\n\"Actions\" in GitHub are reusable commands or tasks to run inside a job. However, they are written for execution inside a Docker container or coded as individual steps using JavaScript. This adds additional work and limits the scope in which they can be applied.\n\nCircleCI offers similar functionality in our [orbs](https://circleci.com/docs/orbs/use/orb-intro/). The primary difference is that CircleCI orbs are just packaged, reusable YAML, so you can create orbs with reusable jobs, executors, or commands, and use them however you see fit in any of your jobs or workflows.\n\nGitHub offers browsing of Actions in their Marketplace; CircleCI has an [Orb Registry](https://circleci.com/developer/orbs) as well as an [Integrations Page](https://circleci.com/integrations/) containing numerous Certified, Partner, and community orbs / integrations.\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#runners-vs-executors)Runners vs. executors\n\nIn GitHub, you can specify your builds to run in Linux, macOS, and Windows environments via a `runs-on` key in the YAML, and if you want to run anything in a container, you specify an additional `container` key.\n\nIn CircleCI, you have the same choice of environments (called Executors), with additional options and features for Docker.\n\nFor each of the [executor types](https://circleci.com/docs/executor-intro/), you have a choice of different versions which will subsequently have various versions of base software installed.\n\nSee the table in the next section to compare configuration.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#configuration-comparison)Configuration comparison\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n**Using Docker?** Authenticating Docker pulls from image registries is recommended when using the Docker execution environment. Authenticated pulls allow access to private Docker images, and may also grant higher rate limits, depending on your registry provider. For further information see [Using Docker authenticated pulls](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execution-managed/private-images/).\n\n| GitHub Config | CircleCI Config |\n| --- | --- |\n| Specifying execution environment. While container execution is specified separately in GitHub, `docker` is its [own class of executor](https://circleci.com/docs/configuration-reference/#docker-machine-macos-windows-executor) in CircleCI. |\n| ``` # Choosing an Operating System runs-on: ubuntu-latest # or windows, etc. # If running steps on a container container: image: openjdk:17.0-jdk ``` yaml | ``` # Docker (container) Executor docker: - image: cimg/openjdk:17.0 # Linux Ubuntu Executor machine: image: ubuntu-2004:202010-01 # macOS Executor macos: xcode: 14.2.0 # Windows Executor machine: image: 'windows-server-2022-gui:current' resource_class: windows.medium # can be medium, large, xlarge, 2xlarge ``` yaml |\n| Specifying dependencies/services. All images specified after the first in CircleCI are treated [as dependencies](https://circleci.com/docs/configuration-reference/#docker). |\n| ``` jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest # Main container container: image: openjdk:17.0-jdk # Dependency Service(s) services: postgres: image: postgres:10.8 env: POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres POSTGRES_DB: postgres ``` yaml | ``` jobs: build: docker: # Primary Executor - image: cimg/openjdk:17.0 # Dependency Service(s) - image: postgres:10.8 environment: POSTGRES_USER: postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres POSTGRES_DB: postgres ``` yaml |\n| Specifying steps to [run](https://circleci.com/docs/configuration-reference/#run) in a job. Similar functionality, different syntax. |\n| ``` jobs: build: # runner config here steps: - name: Build with Gradle run: ./gradlew build ``` yaml | ``` jobs: build: # executor config here steps: - run: name: Build with Gradle command: ./gradlew build ``` yaml |\n| Using shared tasks (Actions for GitHub, orbs for CircleCI). In CircleCI, you declare orbs at the top level and then [refer to them by name in config](https://circleci.com/docs/configuration-reference/#orbs), similar in concept to Python or JavaScript imports. |\n| ``` jobs: build: # runner config here steps: - name: Slack Notify uses: rtCamp/action-slack-notify@v1.0.0 env: SLACK_COLOR: '#32788D' SLACK_MESSAGE: 'Tests passed' SLACK_TITLE: Slack Notify GA SLACK_USERNAME: Bobby SLACK_WEBHOOK: # WEBHOOK ``` yaml | ``` orbs: slack-orb: circleci/slack@3.4.0 jobs: build: # executor config here steps: - slack-orb/notify: color: '#32788D' message: Tests passed title: Testing Slack Orb author_name: Bobby webhook: # WEBHOOK ``` yaml |\n| Using conditional steps in the workflow. CircleCI offers the following: * [Basic conditions on steps, using the `when` attribute](https://circleci.com/docs/reference/configuration-reference/#the-when-attribute) (for example, `on_success` [default], `always`, `on_failure`). * [Conditional steps](https://circleci.com/docs/configuration-reference/#the-when-step) based on parameters. * [Conditional jobs](https://circleci.com/docs/reusing-config/#using-the-parameters-declaration). * Conditional, parameterized [workflows](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/orchestrate/workflows/#use-conditional-logic-in-workflows). |\n| ``` jobs: build: # environment config here steps: - name: My Failure Step run: echo \"Failed step\" if: failure() - name: My Always Step run: echo \"Always step\" if: always() ``` yaml | ``` jobs: build: # executor config here steps: - run: name: My Failure Step command: echo \"Failed step\" when: on_fail - run: name: My Always Step command: echo \"Always step\" when: always ``` yaml |\n\nFor more configuration examples on CircleCI, visit our [Examples and Guides Overview](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/examples-and-guides-overview/) and [Example Projects](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/sample-config/) pages.\n\nSince the configuration between GitHub Actions and CircleCI is similar, it should be fairly trivial to migrate your jobs and workflows. However, for best chances of success, we recommend migrating over items in the following order:\n\n1.   [Jobs, Steps, and Workflows](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/about-circleci/concepts/)\n\n2.   [More Advanced Workflow and Job Dependency Configuration](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/orchestrate/workflows/)\n\n3.   [Actions to Orbs](https://circleci.com/docs/orbs/use/orb-intro/). Our registry can be found [here](https://circleci.com/developer/orbs?filterBy=all).\n\n4.   [Optimizations like caching, workspaces, and parallelism](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/optimize/optimizations/)\n\n### On This Page\n\n*   [Concepts](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#concepts)\n*   [Jobs and workflows](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#jobs-and-workflows)\n*   [Actions vs. orbs](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#actions-vs-orbs)\n*   [Runners vs. executors](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#runners-vs-executors)\n*   [Configuration comparison](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/migrate/migrating-from-github/#configuration-comparison)\n\n#### Suggest an edit to this page\n\n*   [Make a contribution](https://github.com/circleci/circleci-docs/edit/main/docs/guides/modules/migrate/pages/migrating-from-github.adoc)\n*   [Learn how to contribute](https://github.com/circleci/circleci-docs/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)\n\n#### Still need help?\n\n*   [Ask the CircleCI community](https://discuss.circleci.com/)\n*   [Join the research community](https://circleci.com/research/)\n*   [Visit our support site](https://support.circleci.com/hc/en-us/)\n\n![Image 15: CircleCI Logo](https://circleci.com/docs/_/img/logo.svg)![Image 16: CircleCI Logo](https://circleci.com/docs/_/img/logo-dark.svg)\n\n*   © CircleCI, Inc. toolkit\n*   CLI\n\nInstall and configure the CircleCI local CLI\n============================================\n\n[7 days ago](https://github.com/circleci/circleci-docs/commit/e1fa9113d2ac28b12272ff30323754a04cc32737)\n\nCloud Server v4+\n\nMarkdown\n*   [View markdown](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/index.md)\n*    Copy markdown \n\n### On This Page\n\n*   [The CircleCI CLI and the task runner](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#the-circleci-cli-and-the-task-runner)\n*   [Installation](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#installation)\n*   [Linux install with Snap](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#linux-install-with-snap)\n*   [macOS install with Homebrew](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#macos-install-with-homebrew)\n*   [Windows install with Chocolatey](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#windows-install-with-chocolatey)\n*   [Alternative installation method](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#alternative-installation-method)\n*   [Manual install](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#manual-download)\n*   [Updating the CLI](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#updating-the-cli)\n*   [Updating the legacy CLI](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#updating-the-legacy-cli)\n*   [Configure the CLI](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#configure-the-cli)\n*   [Telemetry](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#telemetry)\n*   [Uninstall](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#uninstallation)\n*   [Next steps](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#next-steps)\n*   [CLI articles in the support centre](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#useful-links)\n*   [Troubleshooting](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#troubleshooting)\n\nThe [CircleCI local command line interface (CLI)](https://circleci-public.github.io/circleci-cli/) brings CircleCI’s advanced and powerful tools to your terminal.\n\nSome of the things you can do with the CLI include:\n\n*   [Debug and validate your CircleCI configuration](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/how-to-use-the-circleci-local-cli/#validate-a-circleci-config)\n\n*   [Run jobs locally](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/how-to-use-the-circleci-local-cli/#run-a-job-in-a-container-on-your-machine)\n\n*   Query CircleCI’s API\n\n*   [Create, publish, view, and manage orbs](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/how-to-use-the-circleci-local-cli/#orb-development-kit)\n\n*   [Manage contexts](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/how-to-use-the-circleci-local-cli/#context-management)\n\nThis page covers the installation and usage of the CircleCI local CLI. The expectation is you have basic knowledge of CI/CD and [CircleCI’s concepts](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/about-circleci/concepts/). You should already have a CircleCI account, an account with a supported VCS.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#the-circleci-cli-and-the-task-runner)The CircleCI CLI and the task runner\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nThe CircleCI local CLI\nThe development tool used on your local machine for day-to-day development tasks. It handles testing and local workflow management.\n\nCircleCI environment CLI\nA specialized command-line interface that retrieves and configures a task. It manages the execution of the job within a chosen compute environment.\n\nBoth tools may share some conceptual similarities. However, they serve different purposes and operate in different contexts with different capabilities and permissions.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#installation)Installation\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nInstall the CircleCI CLI using one of the methods described below.\n\nIf you have previously installed CLI prior to October 2018, you may need to do an extra one-time step to switch to the new CLI. See the [upgrade instructions](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#updating-the-legacy-cli).\n\nFor the majority of installations, we recommend one of the package managers outlined in the sections below to install the CircleCI CLI.\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#linux-install-with-snap)Linux install with Snap\n\nThe following commands will install the CircleCI CLI, Docker, and both the security and auto-update features that come along with [Snap packages](https://snapcraft.io/).\n\n```\nsudo snap install docker circleci\nsudo snap connect circleci:docker docker\n```\n\nshell\n\nWith snap packages, the Docker command will use the Docker snap, not a version of Docker you may have previously installed. For security purposes, snap packages can only read/write files from within `$HOME`.\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#macos-install-with-homebrew)macOS install with Homebrew\n\nIf you are using [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) with macOS, you can install the CLI with the following command:\n\n`brew install circleci`\n\nshell\n\nIf you already have Docker for Mac installed, you can use this command instead:\n\n`brew install --ignore-dependencies circleci`\n\nshell\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#windows-install-with-chocolatey)Windows install with Chocolatey\n\nFor Windows users, CircleCI provides a [Chocolatey](https://chocolatey.org/) package:\n\n`choco install circleci-cli -y`\n\nshell\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#alternative-installation-method)Alternative installation method\n\n**Mac and Linux:**\n\n`curl -fLSs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/main/install.sh | bash`\n\nshell\n\nBy default, the CircleCI CLI tool will be installed to the `/usr/local/bin` directory. If you do not have write permissions to `/usr/local/bin`, you may need to run the above command with `sudo` after the pipe and before `bash`:\n\n`curl -fLSs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/main/install.sh | sudo bash`\n\nshell\n\nYou can also install to an alternate location by defining the `DESTDIR` environment variable when invoking Bash:\n\n`curl -fLSs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/main/install.sh | DESTDIR=/opt/bin bash`\n\nshell\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#manual-download)Manual install\n\nYou can visit the [GitHub releases](https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli/releases) page for the CLI to manually download and install. This approach is best if you would like the installed CLI to be in a specific path on your system.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#updating-the-cli)Updating the CLI\n----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nIf you would just like to check for updates manually (and not install them), use the command:\n\n`circleci update check`\n\nshell\n\nFor **Linux and Windows** installs, you can update to the newest version of the CLI using the following command:\n\n`circleci update`\n\nshell\n\nFor **macOS** installations with Homebrew, you will need to run the following command to update:\n\n`brew upgrade circleci`\n\nshell\n\n### [](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#updating-the-legacy-cli)Updating the legacy CLI\n\nThe newest version of the CLI is a [CircleCI-Public open source project](https://github.com/CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli). If you have the [old CLI installed](https://github.com/circleci/local-cli), run the following commands to update and switch to the new CLI:\n\n```\ncircleci update\ncircleci switch\n```\n\nshell\n\nThis command may prompt you for `sudo` if your user does not have write permissions to the install directory, `/usr/local/bin`.\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#configure-the-cli)Configure the CLI\n------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nBefore using the CLI, you need to generate a CircleCI API token from the [Personal API Token tab](https://app.circleci.com/settings/user/tokens). After you get your token, configure the CLI by running:\n\n`circleci setup`\n\nshell\n\nThe set up process will prompt you for configuration settings. If you are using the CLI with CircleCI cloud, use the default CircleCI host. If you are using CircleCI server, change the value to your installation address (for example, `circleci.your-org.com`).\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#telemetry)Telemetry\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nThe CircleCI CLI includes a telemetry feature that collects basic errors and feature usage data in order to help us improve the experience for everyone.\n\nTelemetry works on an opt-in basis. When running a command for the first time, you will be asked for consent to enable telemetry. Telemetry is disabled by default for non-interactive terminals, ensuring that scripts that leverage the CLI run smoothly.\n\nYou can disable or enable telemetry any time in one of the following ways:\n\n*   Run one of the following commands: `circleci telemetry enable` or `circleci telemetry disable`\n\n*   To disable telemetry, set the `CIRCLECI_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT` environment variable to `1` or `true`\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#uninstallation)Uninstall\n-------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n\nThe commands for uninstalling the CircleCI CLI will vary depending on your original installation method.\n\n**Linux uninstall with Snap**:\n\n`sudo snap remove circleci`\n\nshell\n\n**macOS uninstall with Homebrew**:\n\n`brew uninstall circleci`\n\nshell\n\n**Windows uninstall with Chocolatey**:\n\n`choco uninstall circleci-cli -y --remove dependencies`\n\nshell\n\n**Alternative curl uninstall**: Remove the `circleci` executable from `/usr/local/bin`\n\n[](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/#next-steps)Next Since [[friction-driven module adoption prevents configuration debt by adding complexity only at pain points]], the evolution phase has concrete thresholds: add a module after five manual repetitions of the process it would automate, split a module when its description exceeds 500 characters, remove after three unused sessions, and cap active modules at fifteen to twenty. Because [[composable knowledge architecture builds systems from independent toggleable modules not monolithic templates]], each capability is an independent module with explicit dependencies, so evolution means toggling modules on at these calibrated friction points rather than restructuring a monolithic configuration — the agent adds yaml-schema when structured metadata becomes necessary, processing-pipeline when manual workflows create friction, each addition resolving its own dependencies and composing with everything already active. The agent monitors which note types get used, which fields actually get filled, where navigation fails, where processing produces unlinked notes. Each adaptation traces back to a specific observation mapped to a knowledge graph claim — not intuition but evidence. Since [[schema evolution follows observe-then-formalize not design-then-enforce]], the concrete protocol for schema evolution is a quarterly review with five signals: add a field when 20% of notes manually include it, demote required fields that collect placeholder values, prune unused enums, formalize patterned free text, split MOCs that exceed navigation thresholds. Since [[bootstrapping principle enables self-improving systems]], this phase is bootstrapping in action: the system uses its current capabilities to identify and implement improvements, with each improvement becoming available for the next cycle. And since [[incremental formalization happens through repeated touching of old notes]], the notes themselves are evolving in parallel with the system — claims sharpen, connections densify, vague inklings crystallize — so the system and its content co-evolve. The encoding trajectory mirrors this: since [[methodology development should follow the trajectory from documentation to skill to hook as understanding hardens]], methodology patterns within the system follow their own seed-evolve cycle — seeded as documentation in the context file, evolved through friction encounters into skills, and hardened into hooks when understanding is sufficient.\n./plugins/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:4:topics: [\"[[processing-workflows]]\"]\n./plugins/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:17:The infrastructure itself demonstrates this principle. Since [[live index via periodic regeneration keeps discovery current]], index regeneration should be encoded in hooks or skills rather than run ad-hoc — the quality gate here is ensuring regeneration happens at the right moments without human memory. An agent who manually runs `rg \"^description:\"` gets the same data as a pre-computed index, but misses the guarantee that the index is current. The skill encodes the WHEN as well as the WHAT. But even skills require invocation, and since [[hook enforcement guarantees quality while instruction enforcement merely suggests it]], hooks provide an even deeper enforcement layer — one that fires regardless of whether the agent invokes anything at all. \"workflows\",\n./artifacts/deconflict/profile-cache.json:218863:        \"workflows\",\n./plugins/arscontexta/methodology/stigmergy coordinates agents through environmental traces without direct communication.md:31:The stigmergic principle extends beyond reactive trace-following into proactive territory. Since [[hook-driven learning loops create self-improving methodology through observation accumulation]], the observation-to-rethink loop is stigmergy applied to methodology evolution: observations are traces left by one session that become stimulus for a future rethink phase, with no direct communication between the observing agent and the revising agent. And since [[programmable notes could enable property-triggered workflows]], the paradigm can evolve further — from agents responding to traces they discover toward notes actively soliciting attention based on their properties. A note whose staleness threshold has expired, or whose connection count is anomalously low, can surface itself for maintenance. Since [[session outputs are packets for future selves]], each session should produce composable building blocks that future sessions can assemble from rather than starting from zero. Creation becomes assembly. The system accumulates building blocks. Packets also enable session isolation: since [[LLM attention degrades as context fills]], handoffs through packets preserve attention quality by giving each processing phase fresh context. The handoff documents ARE packets — since [[session handoff creates continuity without persistent memory]], each session's structured summary functions as a briefing packet that the next session assembles from. The session handoff format is a packet specification: completed work, incomplete tasks, discoveries, recommendations — all the building blocks for session N+1 to assemble its context. Because [[the generation effect requires active transformation not just storage]], packets must contain generated artifacts — synthesis, articulated connections, processed insights — not merely collected inputs. A packet of bookmarks has no assembly value. A packet of claims with descriptions and connections enables genuine assembly. The generation is what makes the packet composable. But since [[verbatim risk applies to agents too]], the packet can look generated while actually being reorganized content — a well-formatted summary that adds no insight. The risk for packet-based workflows: agents producing packets at high velocity that appear composable but contain no genuine building blocks inside.\n./plugins/arscontexta/methodology/intermediate packets enable assembly over creation.md:19:This connects to [[processing effort should follow retrieval demand]] at an interesting scale. JIT processing says invest on retrieval, not capture — minimal work upfront, deep processing when something proves valuable. Packets operate one level up: the session itself performs retrieval-driven work, and the packet is the processed output. The packet IS what JIT produces when retrieval triggers deep engagement. enables self-improving systems.md:13:For agent-operated knowledge systems, this means the system should be developed using the system. Agent workflows for research, synthesis, and creation get documented in the system they operate on. When agents discover friction or missing capabilities, they capture that as system evolution opportunities. The system improves because its operators constantly use it and feed back improvements. The tightest version of this loop happens when [[context files function as agent operating systems through self-referential self-extension]] -- the context file that teaches methodology also teaches the agent how to modify that context file, so the recursive improvement operates not just on outputs (notes, skills) but on the operating instructions themselves. This self-modification works without coordination because [[local-first file formats are inherently agent-native]] — the agent needs no authentication or external services to read and write its own skill files. And since [[data exit velocity measures how quickly content escapes vendor lock-in]], this dependency is not just a design intuition but an auditable metric: every feature that lowers exit velocity is a potential bootstrapping bottleneck. If a feature requires proprietary tooling to function, the recursive improvement loop stalls at the boundary of that tool — the system can no longer freely read, modify, and write its own substrate. This works because [[each new note compounds value by creating traversal paths]] — in graph-structured knowledge, improvements don't just add linearly but multiply through new connections. Each skill or workflow improvement becomes a node that increases the value of existing nodes. Since [[session handoff creates continuity without persistent memory]], sessions themselves participate in bootstrapping: each session reads what previous sessions wrote, improves the system, and writes for future sessions. The handoff chain IS the bootstrapping loop at the operational level — no persistent memory needed, just externalized briefings that accumulate improvements.\n./plugins/arscontexta/methodology/bootstrapping principle enables self-improving systems.md:29:Agent-operated knowledge systems implement this principle by treating system documentation, skills, and infrastructure as first-class content to be processed by the same workflows that process external content. Typing is 40-60 wpm for most people. This isn't a marginal improvement — voice capture triples throughput, which means the bottleneck shifts from externalization speed to thinking speed. When you speak, you can externalize as fast as you think, so the capture channel stops being the constraint. This is why AudioPen, Whisper, and similar voice-first workflows have gained traction in agent-delegated knowledge systems: they remove the bottleneck that makes capture feel like work. Because [[cognitive offloading is the architectural foundation for vault design]], every friction point in capture fights the cognitive architecture — and voice eliminates the largest remaining one. When externalization costs less effort than retention, the rational choice is always to offload. Traditional notes are inert — the agent acts on them. Programmable notes are reactive — they influence when and how the agent acts. This shifts the architecture from pull (agent searches for relevant content) to push (content declares its relevance). The shift is especially important because since [[prospective memory requires externalization]], every \"remember to check this note later\" intention is a guaranteed failure across agent sessions. Property-triggered workflows eliminate the prospective memory demand entirely — the note surfaces itself when conditions are met, rather than depending on any agent to remember that attention is due. Since [[dangling links reveal which notes want to exist]], the vault already has notes that \"want\" things — this pattern extends that: notes that want attention, want review, want connection. This connects to [[bootstrapping principle enables self-improving systems]]: property-triggered workflows let the vault participate in its own maintenance by declaring what needs attention. The system improves itself through the notes it contains.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/programmable notes could enable property-triggered workflows.md:41:The risk is complexity. Every property trigger is a rule; rules interact; interactions create surprises. A note might trigger multiple workflows simultaneously. Staleness-based surfacing seems high-value (prevents write-only memory). Due-date surfacing seems high-value (explicit scheduling). Status-transition triggers seem medium-value (could automate parts of the processing pipeline). Arbitrary programmability seems low-value (complexity exceeds benefit for most workflows). The consequence speed framework helps here: triggers earn their complexity when the problem they detect propagates faster than the next scheduled check would catch it. A schema violation that propagates instantly justifies per-event complexity. A staleness condition that develops over weeks does not need event-driven infrastructure — a periodic scan suffices. The guarantee is what makes Gall's Law reliable at the module level: enabling a module cannot corrupt what already works, so the evolutionary add-at-friction-points pattern carries no risk of breaking existing structure. And since [[dependency resolution through topological sort makes module composition transparent and verifiable]], the system can show users exactly what needs to be newly enabled and why — so incremental adoption is not just safe but legible, turning each evolutionary step into an architectural explanation rather than opaque automation. Without the guarantee, incremental adoption would be a gamble rather than a principled design strategy. But Gall's Law also creates the conditions for a subtle failure: since [[implicit dependencies create distributed monoliths that fail silently across configurations]], each module added at a friction point is tested in the context of whatever was already active, so undeclared dependencies on co-active modules form through testing context rather than design intent. The distributed monolith grows one well-tested module at a time — each addition is locally validated against its testing configuration but globally coupled through undeclared field reads and convention assumptions. The current vault architecture wasn't designed — it accumulated. System documentation started as a few paragraphs. Skills emerged when patterns repeated enough to justify extraction — and since [[skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates]], those skills now contain the accumulated learning that couldn't have been designed upfront. The queue system appeared when manual task tracking became friction. Because [[bootstrapping principle enables self-improving systems]], this evolution happens through the system itself: the system writes the skills that process its own content. Gall's Law says where to add complexity (at friction points), bootstrapping says how to add it (using current capabilities).\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/complex systems evolve from simple working systems.md:21:This translates to a concrete development pattern, and since [[four abstraction layers separate platform-agnostic from platform-dependent knowledge system features]], the layers formalize what the phases target: Phase 1 implements foundation (files and text conventions), Phase 2 adds convention (instruction-encoded standards), Phase 3 adds automation only where instruction compliance degrades. The layers make the evolutionary sequence prescriptive rather than intuitive. Phase 1: start with atomic kernel — agents dump content with minimal structure. Phase 2: monitor and log friction — track retrieval failures, navigation confusion, repeated manual work. Phase 3: propose structural fixes only for documented friction points. The key is that phase 3 never runs speculatively. \"Only optimize when the pain of not optimizing exceeds the effort of doing so.\" An agent that starts by building elaborate MOC hierarchies violates this principle; an agent that starts by dumping notes and gradually adding wiki links as connections emerge follows it. The YAGNI principle from Extreme Programming applies directly: do not add functionality until necessary. This prevents premature optimization where systems become complex before they become useful. This provides an alternative failure model to [[PKM failure follows a predictable cycle]]: where that experiment tests whether failure cascades from accumulation (Stage 1 → abandonment), Gall's Law suggests failure might emerge from premature complexity — Stage 4 (Over-engineering) might arise independently from internal complexity pressure rather than cascading from earlier stages. At derivation time this risk intensifies, because since [[premature complexity is the most common derivation failure mode]], a well-developed claim graph justifies each configuration choice individually while the composed system exceeds what users can absorb — a complexity budget constrains initial deployment to the minimum viable configuration above the kernel floor — concretely, two to three note types, two to four MOCs, four or fewer processing phases, and hooks only for the highest-value automation. These numbers are not arbitrary; since [[cognitive offloading is the architectural foundation for vault design]], they represent the threshold below which a user can hold the entire system in working memory while building habits, and above which the system demands more cognitive overhead than the workflows it automates. The budget forces derivation to grow through friction rather than foresight. Dangling links wanting resolution is one instance of a broader pattern: metadata conditions that trigger surfacing behavior.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/derivation generates knowledge systems from composable research claims not template customization.md:25:The enabling condition for derivation is the claim graph itself — a dense, interlinked network where claims about note design connect to claims about linking strategy, which connect to claims about processing workflows, which connect to claims about maintenance cadence. Because [[dense interlinked research claims enable derivation while sparse references only enable templating]], this is not a quality preference but a structural threshold: four specific properties (atomic composability, dense interlinking, methodology provenance, semantic queryability) must be present before derivation can function at all. Since [[four abstraction layers separate platform-agnostic from platform-dependent knowledge system features]], the derivation process is itself layered: foundation-layer choices (files, markdown, wiki links) are universal and require no user input, convention-layer choices (quality standards, naming patterns) depend on use case, automation-layer choices (hooks, skills, pipelines) depend on platform tier, and orchestration-layer choices (multi-phase processing, team coordination) depend on both platform tier and scale. Each layer narrows the audience while deepening the customization.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/composable knowledge architecture builds systems from independent toggleable modules not monolithic templates.md:27:The practical consequence is that since [[complex systems evolve from simple working systems]], composable architecture enables Gall's Law at the feature level. An agent starts with zero modules (just markdown files), adds yaml-schema when it wants structured metadata, adds wiki-links when it wants connections, adds mocs when navigation becomes painful, and adds processing-pipeline when manual workflows create friction. Each addition resolves its own dependencies and composes with everything already active, and since [[progressive schema validates only what active modules require not the full system schema]], the validation layer respects this same incremental logic — a user with only yaml-schema and wiki-links enabled never sees warnings about fields belonging to mocs or processing-pipeline modules they have not yet adopted. This maps directly to [[derived systems follow a seed-evolve-reseed lifecycle]] — the seed phase activates a minimal module set, the evolution phase toggles modules on at friction points, and reseeding reconfigures the module selection when accumulated changes drift the system into incoherence. This is fundamentally different from installing a monolithic template and stripping features away — addition is safer than subtraction because addition exposes exactly what is changing, while subtraction requires understanding what will break. But since [[module deactivation must account for structural artifacts that survive the toggle]], even the additive approach has an asymmetric cost: each module enabled at a friction point creates YAML fields, MOC links, and validation rules that persist if the module is later disabled, so the evolutionary cycle of enabling and disabling modules accumulates ghost infrastructure unless modules define both activation and deactivation behaviors. But even additive adoption requires the user to know WHICH modules to enable first, and since [[use-case presets dissolve the tension between composability and simplicity]], presets bridge this gap by bundling curated module selections under use-case labels — the user selects \"Research Vault\" rather than individually evaluating thirteen modules, and the preset resolves all dimension coupling and dependency chains at once. The composable substrate remains intact underneath: every preset-provided module can be individually toggled after activation, so the preset gives template-level simplicity as an entry point without sacrificing the incremental adoption that composable architecture makes safe.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/hook-driven learning loops create self-improving methodology through observation accumulation.md:4:topics: [\"[[agent-cognition]]\", \"[[processing-workflows]]\"]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/hook-driven learning loops create self-improving methodology through observation accumulation.md:62:- [[processing-workflows]]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/legal case management uses precedent chains with regulatory change propagation.md:693:Four processing workflows, each with distinct legal requirements:\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/legal case management uses precedent chains with regulatory change propagation.md:762:When a new case is briefed, always check [[precedents]] for affected principle notes before filing. The skeleton describes the forward pass but not the backward maintenance that since [[structure without processing provides no value]] demands. The vault addresses this through reweaving — a backward pass that revisits old notes with new understanding — but reweaving does not fit neatly into the four-phase model. Since [[backward maintenance asks what would be different if written today]], reweaving is more like running the skeleton again with a different entry point: instead of starting from capture, you start from an existing note and ask what would be different if processed today. Whether this makes the skeleton a cycle rather than a sequence, or whether backward maintenance is genuinely a different operation, remains an open question worth investigating as more domain implementations emerge. [\"[[processing-workflows]]\"]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/throughput matters more than accumulation.md:58:- [[processing-workflows]]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:4:topics: [\"[[processing-workflows]]\"]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:17:The infrastructure itself demonstrates this principle. Since [[live index via periodic regeneration keeps discovery current]], index regeneration should be encoded in hooks or skills rather than run ad-hoc — the quality gate here is ensuring regeneration happens at the right moments without human memory. An agent who manually runs `rg \"^description:\"` gets the same data as a pre-computed index, but misses the guarantee that the index is current. The skill encodes the WHEN as well as the WHAT. But even skills require invocation, and since [[hook enforcement guarantees quality while instruction enforcement merely suggests it]], hooks provide an even deeper enforcement layer — one that fires regardless of whether the agent invokes anything at all. Skills and hooks form complementary enforcement: skills encode methodology workflows that must be deliberately invoked, hooks encode deterministic checks that fire automatically on events.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:21:And there is a second shadow side: the rationalization trap. Since [[productivity porn risk in meta-system building]] tests whether building sophisticated workflows becomes procrastination disguised as work, the very argument that skills encode methodology (and therefore justify their complexity) could rationalize infinite building. The experiment makes this testable: if system complexity correlates with output velocity, skills justify themselves; if complexity grows while output stays flat, the accumulated learning justification is rationalization.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/skills encode methodology so manual execution bypasses quality gates.md:50:- [[processing-workflows]]\n./utilities/circleci/references/raw-docs-md/docs-guides-getting-started-first-steps-.md:810:Migrate scheduled workflows to schedule triggers\n./utilities/circleci/references/raw-docs-md/docs-guides-getting-started-first-steps-.md:818:Schedule triggers with multiple workflows\n./utilities/circleci/references/raw-docs-md/docs-guides-getting-started-first-steps-.md:3412:.circleci/config.yml\n./skills-system/openai-docs/SKILL.md:21:2. 17](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/toolkit/local-cli/)\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/intermediate packets enable assembly over creation.md:4:topics: [\"[[processing-workflows]]\"]\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/intermediate packets enable assembly over creation.md:15:The implication for agent work: structure outputs for reuse. Since [[session outputs are packets for future selves]], each session should produce composable building blocks that future sessions can assemble from rather than starting from zero. Creation becomes assembly. The system accumulates building blocks. Packets also enable session isolation: since [[LLM attention degrades as context fills]], handoffs through packets preserve attention quality by giving each processing phase fresh context. The handoff documents ARE packets — since [[session handoff creates continuity without persistent memory]], each session's structured summary functions as a briefing packet that the next session assembles from. The session handoff format is a packet specification: completed work, incomplete tasks, discoveries, recommendations — all the building blocks for session N+1 to assemble its context. Because [[the generation effect requires active transformation not just storage]], packets must contain generated artifacts — synthesis, articulated connections, processed insights — not merely collected inputs. A packet of bookmarks has no assembly value. A packet of claims with descriptions and connections enables genuine assembly. The generation is what makes the packet composable. But since [[verbatim risk applies to agents too]], the packet can look generated while actually being reorganized content — a well-formatted summary that adds no insight. The risk for packet-based workflows: agents producing packets at high velocity that appear composable but contain no genuine building blocks inside.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/intermediate packets enable assembly over creation.md:19:This connects to [[processing effort should follow retrieval demand]] at an interesting scale. JIT processing says invest on retrieval, not capture — minimal work upfront, deep processing when something proves valuable. Packets operate one level up: the session itself performs retrieval-driven work, and the packet is the processed output. The packet IS what JIT produces when retrieval triggers deep engagement. Packets don't contradict JIT; they're what JIT workflows naturally create.\n./product/domain/arscontexta/methodology/intermediate packets enable assembly over creation.md:52:- [[processing-workflows]]\n./skills-system/openai-docs/references/latest-model.md:16:| `gpt-5.3-codex` | Agentic coding, code editing, and tool-heavy coding workflows |\n./skills-system/openai-docs/references/latest-model.md:17:| `gpt-5.1-codex-mini` | Cheaper coding workflows |\n./skills-system/openai-docs/references/latest-model.md:25:| `gpt-audio-mini` | Cheaper Chat Completions audio workflows |\n./product/domain/agent-native-architecture/SKILL.md:33:The surprising discovery: **a really good coding agent is actually a really good general-purpose agent.** The same architecture that lets Codex refactor a codebase can let an agent organize your files, manage your reading list, or automate your workflows.\n./product/domain/agent-native-architecture/SKILL.md:235:- agent-as-router designs where the agent only picks prewritten workflows;\n./product/domain/agent-native-architecture/SKILL.md:250:- tools stay atomic and features are expressed as outcomes, not hand-coded workflows;\n./utilities/notebooklm/SKILL.md:3:description: Run NotebookLM workflows for notebook management, question answering, and audio or video overviews.
